Anathema.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Anathema.}}''Anáthema'', by v{{ls}}e of Scripture is either that vvhich by {{ls}}eparation from profane v{{ls}}e, and by dedication to God, is holy, dreadful, and not vulgarly to be touched: or contrarievvi{{ls}}e, that which is reiected, {{ls}}euered, or abandoned from God, as cur{{ls}}ed and dete{{ls}}ted, and therfore is to be auoided. Paul wi{{ls}}heth to be anathema.}}Novv how the Apo{{ls}}tle, vvi{{ls}}hing him {{ls}}elf to be Anathema from Chri{{ls}}t to {{ls}}aue his Countrie mens {{ls}}oules, did take this vvord, it is a very hard thing to determine. Some thinke, he de{{ls}}ired onely to die for their {{ls}}aluation. Others, that being very loth to be kept from the fruition of Chri{{ls}}t, yet he could be content to be {{ls}}o {{ls}}till for to {{ls}}aue their {{ls}}oules. Others, that he vvi{{ls}}hed vvhat malediction or {{ls}}eparation from Chri{{ls}}t {{ls}}o euer that did not imply the disfauour of God tovvards him, nor take avvay his loue toward God. This only is certaine that it is a point of vn{{ls}}peakable charitie in the Apo{{ls}}tles brea{{ls}}t, and a paterne to al Bi{{ls}}hops and Prie{{ls}}ts, hovv to loue the {{ls}}aluation of their flocke. As the like vvas vttered by Moy{{ls}}es vvhen he {{ls}}aid, {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=''Exo. 32, 32''.}}''Either forgiue this people, or blot me out of thy booke''.

Not al of I{{ls}}rael.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Gods promis not made to carnal I{{ls}}rael.}}Though the people of the Ievves vvere many waies honoured and priuiledged, and namely by Chri{{ls}}tes taking fle{{ls}}h of them: yet the promis of grace and {{ls}}aluation was neither onely made to them, nor to al them that carnally came of them or their fathers: Gods election and mercie depending vpon his owne purpo{{ls}}e, vvil, and determination, and not tied to any nation, familie, or per{{ls}}on.

But in I{{ls}}aac.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=I{{ls}}aac preferred before I{{ls}}mael.}}The promi{{ls}}{{ls}}e made to Abraham was not in I{{ls}}mael, vvho vvas a {{ls}}onne borne onely by fle{{ls}}h and nature: but in I{{ls}}aac, vvho vvas a {{ls}}onne obtained by promi{{ls}}{{ls}}e, faith, and miracle: and vvas a figure of the Churches children borne to God in Bapti{{ls}}me.

Of one copulation.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Iacob before E{{ls}}au.}}It is proued al{{ls}}o by Gods choo{{ls}}ing of Iacob before E{{ls}}au (who vvere not onely brethren by father and mother, but al{{ls}}o tvvinnes, and E{{ls}}au the elder of the two, vvhich according to carnal count {{ls}}hould haue had the preeminence) that God in giuing graces folovveth not the temporal or carnal prerogatiues of men or families.

''11. Not yet borne.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=By the example of Iacob and E{{ls}}au, is {{ls}}hewed Gods mere mercie in the elect, and iu{{ls}}tice in the reprobate.}}By the {{ls}}ame example of tho{{ls}}e twinnes, it is euident al{{ls}}o, that neither nations nor particular per{{ls}}ons be elected eternally, or called temporally, or preferred to Gods fauour before others, by their ovvne merites: becau{{ls}}e God, vvhen he made choi{{ls}}e, and fir{{ls}}t loued Iacob, and refu{{ls}}ed E{{ls}}au, re{{ls}}pected them both as il, and the one no le{{ls}}{{ls}}e then the other guilty of damnation for original {{ls}}inne, vvhich vvas alike in them both. And therfore vvhere iu{{ls}}tly he might haue reprobated both, he {{ls}}aued of mercie one. Which one therfore, being as il and as void of good as the other, mu{{ls}}t hold of Gods eternal purpo{{ls}}e, mercie, and election, that he was preferred before his brother vvhich was elder then him {{ls}}elf, and no wor{{ls}}e them him {{ls}}elf. And his brother E{{ls}}au on the other {{ls}}ide hath no cau{{ls}}e to complaine, for that God neither did nor {{ls}}uffered any thing to be done towards him, that his {{ls}}inne did not de{{ls}}erue, for although God elect eternally & giue his fir{{ls}}t grace without al merites, yet he doth not reprobate or hate any man but for {{ls}}inne, or the fore{{ls}}ight thereof.

''14. Is there iniquitie.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Prede{{ls}}tination and reprobation take not away free wil, neither mu{{ls}}t any man be retchle{{ls}}{{ls}}e & de{{ls}}perate.}}Vpon the former di{{ls}}cour{{ls}}e that of tvvo per{{ls}}ons equal, God calleth the one to mercie, and leaueth the other in his {{ls}}inne, one might inferre that God were vniu{{ls}}t and an accepter of per{{ls}}ons. To vvhich the Apo{{ls}}tle an{{ls}}vvereth, that God vvere not iu{{ls}}t nor indifferent in deede, {{ls}}o to v{{ls}}e the matter where grace or {{ls}}aluation vvere due. As if two men being Chri{{ls}}tened, both beleeue wel, & liue vvel: if God {{ls}}hould giue heauen to the one, & {{ls}}hould damne the other, then were he vniu{{ls}}t, partial, & forgetful of his promi{{ls}}{{ls}}e: but re{{ls}}pecting or taking two, who both be vvorthy of damnation (as al are before they be fir{{ls}}t called to mercie) then the matter {{ls}}tandeth on mere mercie, and of the giuers wil and liberalitie, in which ca{{ls}}e partialitie hath no place.
